1.q: אֶת־כָּל־חֵיל֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וּ⁠שְׁנַ֥יִם מֶ֛לֶךְ אִתּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠ס֣וּס וָ⁠רָ֑כֶב
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Ben Hadad brought his horses and chariots with the information that he gathered **all of his army**. Alternate translation: [all of his army and horse and chariot, and 32 kings with him]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and there were 32 kings with him]

In this verse, the words **horse and chariot** are singular in form, but they refer to all of Ben Hadad’s horses and chariots as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [and horses and chariots]
See how you translated the similar expression “he has gone down” in 1:25. Alternate translation: [And he went]

While the pronoun **it** refers to the city of Samaria, the author is using that city to represent its defenders. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he fought with the Israelite soldiers who were defending it]

3.note: Ben Hadad did not personally speak the words that follow. His messengers spoke them on his behalf. It may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun to indicate this. Alternate translation: [and they said to him]

3.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר בֶּן־הֲדַ֔ד כַּסְפְּ⁠ךָ֥ וּֽ⁠זְהָבְ⁠ךָ֖ לִֽ⁠י־ה֑וּא וְ⁠נָשֶׁ֧י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בָנֶ֛י⁠ךָ הַ⁠טּוֹבִ֖ים לִ⁠י־הֵֽם
3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Ben Hadad says that your silver and your gold are his, and your best wives and sons are his]

3.q: כַּסְפְּ⁠ךָ֥ וּֽ⁠זְהָבְ⁠ךָ֖ לִֽ⁠י־ה֑וּא וְ⁠נָשֶׁ֧י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בָנֶ֛י⁠ךָ הַ⁠טּוֹבִ֖ים לִ⁠י־הֵֽם
3.note: Ben Hadad assumes that King Ahab will know that he is making a demand backed by the threat of military force. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [If you do not give me your silver and your gold and your best wives and sons, I will destroy this city]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both male and female children. If it would be helpful to your readers, here and in verses 5 and 7 you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both male and female children. Alternate translation: [and your sons and daughters] or [and your children]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:28. Alternate translation: [answered]
Here, **word** represents what Ben Hadad said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Just as you have said]

5.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֥ר בֶּן־הֲדַ֖ד לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כַּסְפְּ⁠ךָ֧ וּ⁠זְהָבְ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠נָשֶׁ֥י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בָנֶ֖י⁠ךָ לִ֥⁠י תִתֵּֽן
5.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the messengers said (level 1). The messengers are quoting what Ben Hadad has told them to say (level 2). This includes a quotation of something that Ben Hadad said previously (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a second-level or third-level quotation.

5.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֥ר בֶּן־הֲדַ֖ד לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כַּסְפְּ⁠ךָ֧ וּ⁠זְהָבְ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠נָשֶׁ֥י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בָנֶ֖י⁠ךָ לִ֥⁠י תִתֵּֽן
5.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Ben Hadad says that he indeed sent to you and told you that you were to give him your silver and your gold and your wives and your sons]

6.note: Ben Hadad is using one part of Ahab, his **eyes**, to mean all of him in the act of desiring valuable possessions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every desire of yours]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything that you desire] or [everything in which you delight]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will take into their possession] or [they will seize]

7.note: Ahab is using **know and see** as a common expression of his culture to mean “consider carefully.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 24:13. Alternate translation: [consider carefully]
Here, the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

8.note: The terms **hear** and **consent** mean similar things, since in this context “hear” means “agree.” The elders and people are using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Do not agree at all]

9.q: אִמְר֞וּ לַֽ⁠אדֹנִ֤⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֨חְתָּ אֶל־עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֤ בָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנָה֙ אֶעֱשֶׂ֔ה וְ⁠הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה לֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל לַ⁠עֲשׂ֑וֹת
9.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell my lord the king that all he sent to his servant at first, I will do, but this thing I am not able to do]

Ahab is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your servant,]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **first**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [originally]

Here, **word** represents what the messengers said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and reported to Ben Hadad what Ahab had said]

10.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשׂ֥וּ⁠ן לִ֛⁠י אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְ⁠כֹ֣ה יוֹסִ֑פוּ אִם־יִשְׂפֹּק֙ עֲפַ֣ר שֹׁמְר֔וֹן לִ⁠שְׁעָלִ֕ים לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ⁠רַגְלָֽ⁠י
10.note: Following the custom of this culture, Ben Hadad is swearing an oath by stating a condition and the consequence he is asking the gods to make happen if the condition is met. He is stating the consequence before the condition. If it would be helpful to your readers, in your translation, you could state the condition before the consequence. See how you translated the similar expression in 19:2. Alternate translation: [If the dust of Samaria is enough for handfuls for all of the people who are at my feet, thus may the gods do to me, and thus may they add]
See how you translated the similar expression “and thus may he add” in 2:23. Alternate translation: [and may they do even worse]
In this context, the term **people** refers to the soldiers in Ahab’s army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the soldiers]

Ben Hadad is using his **feet** to represent his soldiers walking where he has just walked. In other words, they are following him, and this represents that he is their military commander. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If you have already translated the book of Judges, see how you translated the similar expression in Judges 4:10. Alternate translation: [who are under my command]

11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell him that one girding should not boast like one ungirding]
The implied “you” in the imperative **Tell** is plural here because Ahab is addressing the messengers of Ben Hadad. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

12.note: Here, **this word** represents what Ahab had the messengers tell Ben Hadad said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this reply]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. Ben Hadad’s overconfidence and complacency help lead to his defeat in this battle. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Ben Hadad is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [“Set yourselves in array!” And they set themselves in array against the city] or [“Form battle lines!” And they formed battle lines against the city]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:7. Alternate translation: [And just then]

13.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הְֽ⁠רָאִ֔יתָ אֵ֛ת כָּל־הֶ⁠הָמ֥וֹן הַ⁠גָּד֖וֹל הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה הִנְ⁠נִ֨י נֹתְנ֤⁠וֹ בְ⁠יָֽדְ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠יּ֔וֹם וְ⁠יָדַעְתָּ֖ כִּֽי־אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה
13.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that though you have certainly seen all of this great multitude, behold him, giving it into your hand today, and you will know that he is Yahweh]

The prophet is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have certainly seen all of this great multitude]
See how you translated the similar expression “behold you, seeking” in 11:22. Alternate translation: [I am about to give it]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into your power]

14.note: Ahab and the prophet are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [By whom will Yahweh give this multitude into my hand … I will give it into your hand by the servants of the leaders of the districts]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that he will do that by the servants of the leaders of the districts]

Having the **servants of the leaders of the districts** lead the attack was a symbolic action that showed that Yahweh would win this battle for the Israelites, since these were the youngest and least experienced soldiers. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [By the young, inexperienced servants of the district leaders, so that it will be clear that I am winning this battle for you]

Ahab is using **Who will bind the battle** as a common expression of his culture to mean “Who will begin the battle” or “Who will start the attack.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Who will begin the engagement] or [Who will attack first]

15.note: See how you translated the same expression in [6:1](ta:06). In this case, the phrase refers specifically to Israelite soldiers, not to the Israelites generally. Alternate translation: [the Israelite soldiers]

17.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ben Hadad sent men to investigate]
In a context such as this, here and through verse 21, your language might say “came” instead of **gone**. Alternate translation: [Men have come out from Samaria]

20.note: The author is using **a man his man** as a common expression of his culture to mean that each of the young Israelite soldiers killed an enemy soldier who confronted him. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And each one struck his opponent]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:15. Alternate translation: [And they killed]

21.note: In this verse, the words **horse** and **chariot** are singular in form, but they refer to all of Ben Hadad’s horses and chariots. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [and he struck the horses and the chariots]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See how you translated the term “struck” in 8:33. Alternate translation: [And he inflicted a severe defeat on Aram]

22.note: The author assumes that readers will know **the prophet** refers to the same prophet who earlier told King Ahab how to defeat the Aramean army. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the prophet who had spoken to Ahab earlier]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:13. Alternate translation: [Take action]
See how you translated the similar expression in 20:7. Alternate translation: [and consider carefully]

The prophet is using **at the return of the year** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in the spring” or “at the beginning of the new agricultural year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [next spring]

23.note: The servants are using these phrases to represent that the Israelites, supposedly because **gods of the hills** made them **stronger** than the Arameans, defeated them in the recent battle, but that if they fought on a **plain**, the Arameans would be **stronger** and so defeat them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language here and in verse 25. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 17:50. Alternate translation: [they defeated us … we will defeat them]

24.note: Ben Hadad’s officials are using **a man from his place** as a common expression of their culture to mean “each one from his position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each one from his position]

25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:4. Alternate translation: [And for your part, you shall muster`]

The officials are speaking of Ben Hadad’s previous army as **having fallen** as a common expression of their culture to mean that this army was destroyed. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [like the army that you lost] or [like the army that the Israelites destroyed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:8. Alternate translation: [And he agreed with what they said]

26.note: The author is using the phrase translated as **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the similar expression in 20:22. Alternate translation: [the next spring]

27.note: The expressions **were mustered** and **were sustained** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ahab mustered the sons of Israel and sustained them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **two little flocks of goats** are small in number, so the Israelite army was small in number compared to the large Aramean army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in relatively small numbers, like two little flocks of goats]

The author says **Aram filled the land** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the Aramean army spread out over much of the land]

28.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה יַ֠עַן אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמְר֤וּ אֲרָם֙ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָרִים֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לֹֽא־אֱלֹהֵ֥י עֲמָקִ֖ים ה֑וּא וְ֠⁠נָתַתִּי אֶת־כָּל־הֶ⁠הָמ֨וֹן הַ⁠גָּ֤דוֹל הַ⁠זֶּה֙ בְּ⁠יָדֶ֔⁠ךָ וִֽ⁠ידַעְתֶּ֖ם כִּֽי־אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה
28.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the **man of God** said to Ahab. (level 1). The man of God is quoting what Yahweh told him to tell Ahab. (level 2). This includes a quotation of something that the Arameans have said previously (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a second-level or third-level quotation.

28.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה יַ֠עַן אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמְר֤וּ אֲרָם֙ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָרִים֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לֹֽא־אֱלֹהֵ֥י עֲמָקִ֖ים ה֑וּא וְ֠⁠נָתַתִּי אֶת־כָּל־הֶ⁠הָמ֨וֹן הַ⁠גָּ֤דוֹל הַ⁠זֶּה֙ בְּ⁠יָדֶ֔⁠ךָ וִֽ⁠ידַעְתֶּ֖ם כִּֽי־אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה
28.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that because Aram has said that he is a god of hills but not a god of valleys, he will give all of this great multitude into your hand, and you will know that he is Yahweh]
Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into your power]

29.q: וַֽ⁠יַּחֲנ֧וּ אֵ֦לֶּה נֹ֥כַח אֵ֖לֶּה שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים
29.note: The author is using **these opposite these** as a common expression of his culture to mean “opposite each other” or “in opposing positions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they camped opposite each other for seven days]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **seventh**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on day seven] or [after seven days]

The author is using **the battle approached** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the armies advanced against each other” or “the battle began.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that the battle was joined] or [that the armies advanced against each other]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:33. Alternate translation: [defeated]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they killed 100,000 foot soldiers in one day]

30.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he hid in a chamber in a chamber]

The phrase **a chamber in a chamber** describes an inner room within another room, likely referring to the most secluded or private area of a building. If your readers would not be familiar with rooms that have other rooms inside them, you could use a more general term or explain the arrangement in a footnote. Alternate translation: [an inner room] or [a private room]

31.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are merciful kings]

Wearing **sackcloth** was a symbolic action by which Ben Hadad’s officials showed humility before the king of Israel. Putting **ropes** on their **heads** was a symbolic action by which they showed that they were willing to become his captives. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [let us put sackcloth on our loins to show humility and ropes on our heads to show that we are willing to become captives]

The officials are using one part of Ben Hadad, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of having his life spared. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [he will let you live]

32.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Your servant Ben Hadad asks you please to let his soul live]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:13. Alternate translation: [He is my fellow king] or [He is my ally]

33.note: The author is speaking of Ben Hadad’s officials as if they were actually **observing signs**, that is, trying to tell fortunes or see omens, when they were listening carefully to Ahab’s words to determine his attitude toward their king. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the men were watching Ahab closely]

The phrase **hastened and caught** expresses a single idea. The word **hastened** tells in what way the officials **caught** or noticed and repeated what Ahab said. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [and they quickly caught]

The implication is that Ben Hadad’s officials are quickly correcting their earlier description of Ben Hadad as Ahab’s “servant” based on Ahab’s reference to him as his “brother.” You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yes, we meant your brother Ben Hadad]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [Go ahead]

Bringing Ben Hadad up onto his **chariot** was a symbolic action by which Ahab showed that he was treating Ben Hadad as an equal and an honored guest rather than as a defeated enemy. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he brought him up onto his chariot to welcome and honor him]

34.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Ben Hadad, while the pronoun **him** refers to Ahab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Ben Hadad said to Ahab]

This is a direct quotation of what Ahab said in response to Ben Hadad. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ahab replied, “And I, I will send you away with a covenant.”]
See how you translated the similar expression “I, I will do” in 5:8. Alternate translation: [And for my part, I will send you away]

In the first clause, the pronoun **he** refers to Ben Hadad, while the pronoun **him** refers to Ahab. In the second clause, the pronoun **he** refers to Ahab, while the pronoun **him** refers to Ben Hadad. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Ben Hadad cut a covenant with Ahab, and Ahab sent Ben Hadad away]

The author is using **cut a covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean that Ben Hadad made a covenant with Ahab. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 5:12. Alternate translation: [And he made a covenant with him]

35.note: The phrase **sons of the prophets** refers to a group of young men whom experienced prophets were training to become prophets. If your readers would not be familiar with what this phrase means, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [from a group of young prophets in training] or [from the prophetic community]

35.q: אָמַ֧ר אֶל־רֵעֵ֛⁠הוּ בִּ⁠דְבַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה הַכֵּ֣י⁠נִי נָ֑א
35.note: The direct quotation may begin after the word **Yahweh** rather than after the word **fellow**. Alternate translation: [said to his fellow by the word of Yahweh, “Strike me, please.”]
Here, **word** represents what Yahweh commanded by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By the command of Yahweh]

36.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the first prophet, while the pronoun **him** refers to the second prophet. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the first man said to the second man]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:8. Alternate translation: [you did not obey the voice of Yahweh]

Here, **voice** represents what Yahweh commanded by using his voice to speak to the first prophet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you did not obey the command of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:22. Alternate translation: [as you leave me, a lion will strike you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:15. Alternate translation: [and a lion will kill you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:29. Alternate translation: [and a lion met him]

39.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he cried out** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to indicate that this action took place at the same time as **the king was passing by**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and just as the king was passing by, he cried out]

The prophet is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [I, your servant,]

39.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר֙ שְׁמֹר֙ אֶת־הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אִם־הִפָּקֵד֙ יִפָּקֵ֔ד וְ⁠הָיְתָ֤ה נַפְשְׁ⁠ךָ֙ תַּ֣חַת נַפְשׁ֔⁠וֹ א֥וֹ כִכַּר־כֶּ֖סֶף תִּשְׁקֽוֹל
39.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And he told me to guard that man. He said that if missing, he was missing, then my life would be in place of his life, or I should pay a kikkar of silver.]

In the story that the prophet is telling, the soldier is repeating forms of the verb **missing** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [If for any reason he is missing]

The soldier in the story is using **your life will be in place of his life** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the prophet would forfeit his own life for allowing the prisoner to escape. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then you will pay for that with your life] or [then we will execute you for letting him get away]
See how you chose to represent the term “kikkars” in 9:14.

40.note: The prophet is saying that he was **doing here and there** as a common expression of his culture to mean that he was “busy with various tasks” or “occupied with other matters.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was doing this and that] or [became preoccupied with other tasks]

By **Thus is your judgment**, the king means that the prophet has pronounced his own judgment by acknowledging that he did exactly what the soldier said would deserve punishment. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I judge you guilty based on your own testimony]

Ahab is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have decided** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of this prophet in presenting the facts of the case in a way that shows he is guilty. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. See how you translated the similar expression “you, you swore” in 1:17. Alternate translation: [you are the one who has decided]

41.note: The phrase **hurried and removed** expresses a single idea. The word **hurried** in what way the prophet **removed** the covering from his eyes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And he hurriedly removed]

42.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה יַ֛עַן שִׁלַּ֥חְתָּ אֶת־אִישׁ־חֶרְמִ֖⁠י מִ⁠יָּ֑ד וְ⁠הָיְתָ֤ה נַפְשְׁ⁠ךָ֙ תַּ֣חַת נַפְשׁ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַמְּ⁠ךָ֖ תַּ֥חַת עַמּֽ⁠וֹ
42.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that because you have sent away a man of his devotion from your hand, so it will be your life in place of his life and your people in place of his people]

Yahweh, speaking through the prophet, is using this possessive form to mean a man whom he had devoted to destruction. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [a man whom I had devoted]

The word that the ULT translates as **devotion** was a specialized term that described the cultural practice of giving something over to Yahweh so that humans would no longer be able to use it. The context indicates that in this case, this was to be accomplished through the total destruction of this **man**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a man whom I wanted you to destroy]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you had him in your power] or [when you had him as your prisoner]
See how you translated the similar expression in 20:39. Alternate translation: [so you will pay for that with your life, and your people will pay for that with their lives]

43.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֧לֶךְ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל עַל־בֵּית֖⁠וֹ סַ֣ר וְ⁠זָעֵ֑ף וַ⁠יָּבֹ֖א שֹׁמְרֽוֹנָ⁠ה
43.note: The author is describing one event, **the king of Israel went to his house**, before describing another event that preceded it, **he came to Samaria**. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [And the king of Israel came to Samaria, and he went to his house sullen and angry]
